reading.body:
The AI Policy Network's five AI lobbying filings name sixteen lobbyists and fifteen bills, a ratio that shows how thinly attention is spread across pending legislation.

The pattern is concentration at the top and a long tail below. Four lobbyists appear on all five filings, five appear on three, and the rest on one or two. The bills are almost entirely distinct, with fifteen separate measures named across five reports. This is not a firm pushing one bill. It is a firm tracking a wide field of AI legislation and assigning overlapping teams to cover it.

For AI specifically, this matters because the policy surface is broadening faster than any single client can engage. The bills named span both chambers and many numbers, which means the firm's client is monitoring AI regulation as a portfolio rather than fighting a single defined threat. That is consistent with an ecosystem where compute buildout, data center siting, and model governance each generate their own legislative tracks.

The data does not say what positions the firm argued, only that it filed. It does not give dollar amounts, committee assignments, or outcomes. It covers five filings and nothing about the firm's other clients or non-AI work. A reader should treat the bill count as a measure of monitoring breadth, not of influence.
